label: ECM
rationale: obs[S1]: ECM 1001, recorded November 1969 at Musikstudio Bauer, Ludwigsburg; produced by Manfred Scheffner with supervision by Manfred Eicher, engineer Kurt Rapp. obs[S2]: Wikipedia confirms personnel Mal Waldron (piano), Isla Eckinger (double bass), Clarence Becton (drums), and recording date 1969-11-24. obs[S3]: AllMusic lists Post-Bop, Piano Jazz, recording date 1969-11-24 at Bauer Studios, Ludwigsburg. obs[S4]: Discogs release 5050263 confirms producer Manfred Scheffner and engineer Kurt Rapp. inf: The album is ECM's first release and a structured, angular piano-trio statement that extends Waldron's hard-bop/post-bop history into the label; its historical weight and musical argument are separable from the ECM imprint.
continuity_case: Waldron's trio language—angular, organized improvisation over song-shaped heads—grows directly out of his hard-bop and song-accompaniment history; the first ECM record is an artist's statement, and I would make the same case if it had appeared on Impulse! or Enja.
scope_flag: ECM gate — 1969, inside window; post-bop/free-jazz piano trio whose free passages are structured rather than atonal; the boundary at issue is whether its grit is canonical or mainly historically significant as ECM's first release.

personnel_record.notes: Supervision by Manfred Eicher per ECM page (S1).

scope_check.boundary_note: It is within the 1940–1979 window but arrives through the newly opened ECM and free-jazz gates; the operative boundary is the bridge test—whether its structured, post-bop-derived freedom genuinely carries 1960s lineage forward rather than relying on its status as ECM 1001.

ballot.case_for: Recorded in 1969 as ECM 1001, the label's first release, this is a historically consequential trio statement rather than merely an archival curiosity (S1). Waldron's angular heads, recurring rhythmic cells, blues-rooted material, and song-shaped structures on pieces such as "Rat Now" and "Rock My Soul" make a credible bridge from his hard-bop/post-bop language into freer European improvisation without abandoning pulse or form. The documented trio—Waldron, Isla Eckinger, and Clarence Becton—makes the record a focused, coherent artist statement whose stark, deliberate sound plausibly anticipates a major strand of ECM's later identity (S1–S3).
ballot.case_against: The dossier establishes recording facts and style tags but supplies virtually no independent evidence of canon-level musical consensus: ECM is a house source, while Wikipedia, AllMusic, and Discogs are principally discographical sources (S1–S4). Its strongest historical claim is its catalogue number, yet the rubric explicitly requires that an ECM record earn itself through continuity and listening value rather than label importance; Waldron's more commonly cited defining records offer stronger personnel networks and broader critical standing. Eckinger and Becton do not provide major session gravity, and the album's austere repetition, grit, and restrained free passages may be less immediately illuminating for a cold listener than central hard-bop or modal piano-trio landmarks.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John treat Free at Last as a bridge-test scope call and audition it for its musical continuity apart from its ECM-first-release significance.
